Chapter Notes

For Phaidei Week 2025, Library.

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Every book in the universe one day ends up at the Library. From simple children’s books to multi-volume epics, from thick biographies to thin travel magazines from worlds far beyond the stars, they all come to Mydei’s desk, and it’s his pleasure to catalog those books. For years, from the rising to the setting of the sun, he has sat at his desk entering those books into the card catalog before passing them off to his librarians to shelve. Though the librarians are the world’s heroes, those brave few willing to venture into the stacks, and the Library rests firmly in the control of the Head Librarian, no one disputes that the Library is his. When someone wants to find a rare tome, they come first to him. 

“Enter,” he says as someone knocks on his door. He closes the book he’s working with—A Midsummer Night’s Dream, by some impossibly named poet from a long-gone, hayseed planet—and looks up from his catalog slate as he removes his glasses.

Hephaestion opens the door, filling it, but he’s hardly broad enough to mask the presence of the man at his back. “A petitioner for the cataloguer,” he says, a smile playing across his lips. He has always found playing at formalities amusing.

Mydei looks past Hephaestion to a silvery-haired young man, eager as a puppy, expression hopeful. It is no small thing to seek out Mydei’s help, and no small expense. While the Library is free to use, the use of its Chief Cataloguer costs several pretty pots of expensive ink. This puppy, wearing a double-breasted suit of white and gold, with accents of blue and gray, looks as though he could hardly afford his own dinner.

“This is Phainon,” Hephaestion continues. “Of Aedes Elysiae.”

A Farmer’s Guide to Aedes Elysiae, Agathinos, Room JJ-319-9.11. The Flora of Aedes Elysiae, Eutychia, Room JL-184-0.254. Fields of Golden Wheat: Aedes Elysiae by Memory, Kleitos, Room M1C-452-7.96.

“Hello, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.” He gestures to the simple, wooden chair in front of his desk. “Tell me of the book you’re seeking.” Some of the other cataloguers, those who aren’t as good at their jobs, will play at pleasantries, but Mydei sees no point. Time is one of man’s many non-renewable resources, and he will waste none of it, neither his nor Phainon’s nor anyone else’s.

As Hephaestion steps out and closes the door, affording them their privacy, Phainon takes up the seat across from Mydei. He folds himself elegantly into it, a gentleman by disposition if not by birth, and sets down a knapsack beside him. His suit is threadbare and worn, the hems around his ankles fraying, his pocket square faded, his gold pocket watch’s chain without luster. There’s an earnestness about his face, a soft kindness at odds with the strange calculation in his eyes—this is the face of a man who drinks bitterness but chooses joy, but Mydei doesn’t find this fascinating. Phainon is almost certainly here for a deceased loved one’s obituary. Even newspapers make their way to the Library. What a waste of ink this task will be.

But Phainon surprises him. “The Lamb and the Sinner,” he says.

Mydei closes his eyes. The Lamb and the Sinner, G.E. Vakulenko, Room UZ-786-8.61. The Lamb and the Sinner, Qin Zihao, Room KP-601-7.38. The Lamb and the Sinner, Ferreira Gullar, Room AL-312-7.11. There are too many. “An author?” he asks.

“Unknown,” Phainon says. “It’s a prosy sort of poetry.”

That narrows the list somewhat. “How does it begin?”

Phainon makes a thoughtful sound. When he speaks again, his voice is lower, softer. Smokey and hypnotic, with a cadence and rhythm that snags at the back of Mydei’s mind. Familiar, in some strange way. “Bundle dried fennel branches tightly, then let it fully soak in olive oil—that is how a handy torch is made,” Phainon says. “Growth, decay, and sprouting once more… They were once unrelated to the civilized world, yet given a name by the unreasonable, and then burned to ashes again.”

That’s all Mydei needs. The Lamb and the Sinner, Unknown, Room QW-398-7.52. He opens his eyes. “I will have my librarians retrieve it. As it’s deep within the Library—”

“I would like to invoke the right of discovery,” Phainon says.

Mydei can’t help himself. He laughs. No one has invoked the right of discovery in his lifetime—nor in hundreds of years preceding it. “Are you a fool or a madman?” he asks, sharp, vicious, uncaring of the force of his verbal blow.

Phainon’s expression, serene and polite, doesn’t change. “Neither.”

“Then you are a liar, and I have no time for those.” He rises from behind his desk. “If that’s all—”

“Silent,” Phainon says, with such weight, such gravity, that Mydei goes still. “Silent, the dawn comes—radiant / Resplendent—the sun rolls up her sleeves / and I / awash in her color, can but breathe dewy morning light.”

Golden sunrise fills Mydei’s office. Petrichor and wet grass suffuse the air, thick on his tongue as he inhales deeply of the moments just after sunrise. Unnatural warmth prickles his skin as it washes over him.

“You are a reader,” Mydei observes. “Why did you not lead with that?”

Phainon makes a helpless gesture. “I didn’t think it was relevant.”

“Your ability to keep yourself alive in the stacks is certainly relevant.” Mydei lowers himself back into his chair. “Why are you not in the emperor’s employ?”

“I find myself ill-suited to following the whims of a tyrant,” Phainon replies blithely, catching Mydei utterly by surprise.

He can’t help himself. He barks out a laugh. “And so, what, you read him such miserable prose that he dismissed you?”

“Something like that.” Phainon shrugs. “Suffice it to say, I won’t be helpless in the stacks. I won’t be dead weight, and you won’t need to protect me and yourself at the same time. I am capable with word and weapon.”

“And your preferred style?”

“Zweihander.”

Mydei reassess the man seated across from him. His poor suit hides his form, disguising muscle as what Mydei mistook for unnecessary bulk. A fighter and a reader. The emperor must have been furious to lose such an asset. “Very well, then,” he says. “I accept your right of discovery.”

Excitement lights Phainon’s face. “When do we leave?” he asks.

“The stacks are not to be tackled lightly. We will need to venture deep into them to find your book, and I will need to make arrangements for my own work. The day after tomorrow.”

“The day after tomorrow,” Phainon says.

The man Mydei meets two days later is nothing like the one who came to his office. Phainon waits for him at Circulation at the front of the Library, where petitioners linger in anticipation of a librarian’s aid. He leans against a gargantuan, three-story pillar of carved, white marble adorned with wrought-iron ivy, but despite his white coat he doesn’t blend in at all. Striking, intense, he cuts a dangerous figure in his leathers, his zweihander sheathed at his side. It, too, leans against the pillar.

A cadre of young women in white shirtwaists and long, navy skirts giggle over him, tittering behind their hands. Either he’s oblivious or pretending not to notice—and Mydei suspects it’s the former, because as soon as Mydei steps around the Circulation desk, Phainon lights up like a gaslamp at dusk. He doesn’t dim even as Mydei’s armored librarians file in behind him, as if Mydei is the sun and Phainon a flower turning toward him.

“I thought it would just be us,” Phainon says, reaching for his zweihander. He buckles the sheath around his waist and sets his hand on the hilt.

“You’re either naively optimistic or overestimating your own capabilities,” Mydei replies dryly. “Venturing into the Library without at least three is suicide.”

Phainon flashes him a grin. “Even with a reader?”

“Even with a reader.” Mydei beckons his librarians forward, introducing them. “Hephaestion, my second. Leonnius, our runner. Ptolemy, who knows the stacks nearly as well as I do. Peucesta, our scout and bard. Perdikkas, our healer. Regardless of your own prowess, if they give you an order, you follow it.”

“Understood,” Phainon says with the conviction of a man who will actually obey. Refreshing, if he will.

“You have supplies?” Mydei asks.

Phainon tugs a strap hanging over his shoulder. “Enough for two days, as you suggested.”

“Good.” Even more refreshing that he’s listened this much already. It’s rare to bring someone into the stacks, but Mydei has heard horror stories from other librarians and cataloguers of men who weighed themselves down with too many supplies and those who, thinking the Library would provide, didn’t bring enough. “Come, then,” he says, and his librarians fall back to allow Phainon a place at his side.

Together, they climb one of the curved staircases that flank the circular Circulation desk. Here, the wings of the Library stretch to either side, where one finds librarians at rest and the offices of the cataloguers, among others, but their destination is immediately in front of them: the caged lifts that descend from the above-ground Library to the heart of the mountain it’s built into. Pairs of armed guards in crisp, red uniforms stand to the side of each lift, their weapons drawn and aimed at the doors.

“Worried about the books escaping?” Phainon asks, with what he obviously assumes is good humor.

Mydei fixes him with a flat look. “No. Not the books.”

Hephaestion and Leonnius step forward, opening the wrought iron doors and holding them to the sides to allow the others entry. Phainon, to his credit, doesn’t balk. He precedes Mydei into the lift. And he takes his cues well from the others, standing in the middle of the lift and well away from the open sides of it. Perhaps this won’t be a miserable expedition.

When they have all found space in the lift, one of the guards steps forward. She salutes Mydei and his librarians. “May the path of knowledge be illuminated before you.” She pulls a lever outside the lift, and the lift begins its smooth descent downwards.

The ambient light disappears quickly as they descend the chiseled chute into the depths of the mountains, illuminated solely by the gaslamp above them. It’s barely enough to see the rock of the walls. Enough light, but not too much.

“Nervous?” Leonnius asks, leaning toward Phainon.

Mydei watches them from the corner of his eyes, his gauntleted arms crossed over his chest.

Phainon laughs, a little too loud in the cramped darkness, and rocks from heel to toe and back again. “A little.”

“Good.” Leonnius knocks him gently on the shoulder. “Only idiots aren’t nervous about a sojourn into the stacks.”

Phainon clears his throat. “Even you?”

“Even me. Even us.” Leonnius puts his hands on his hips and nods toward the glistening rock as they descend, whispering through the darkness. “Been into the Library hundreds of times. Glorious place. Still scares the shit out of me.”

“Scares the shit out of anyone with half a brain,” Peucesta says.

“Can’t believe someone invoked the right of discovery in this day and age,” Leonnius continues. He peers at Phainon. “Did you finalize a will?”

Phainon makes a thin, reedy sound. “Did you?”

“I’m a librarian,” Leonnius says, waving him off. “Of course I have a will.” But his expression is pitying. “You did draft one up?”

“It’s too late to worry about that now,” Phainon says.

“Hell,” Leonnius mutters, and he shoots Mydei a look that screams of annoyance and frustration.

Mydei holds up a forbidding hand. “He invoked the right of discovery.”

“Right, so we just see man to his death?”

“A reader,” Ptolemy interjects. “And one who wields a zweihander.”

“Can he even use it?” Leonnius asks.

Hephaestion rolls his eyes. “If he does, then we haven’t done our jobs. His presence changes nothing.”

“He,” Phainon says, “is literally right here.”

Mydei snaps his fingers twice, and his men fall silent. Hephaestion, Leonnius, Ptolemy, and Peucesta draw their short swords, each of them taking one side of the lift. Perdikkas and Mydei step deeper into the center of the lift, flanking Phainon. “Quiet,” Mydei says to him.

From the darkness comes a soft fluttering, the only warming before a hand shoots from a slotted hole in the rock wall. It’s fast, but Hephaestion is faster, carving the papery hand from its wrist. It floats lazily to the metal floor of the lift, and Phainon stumbles back with a choked, shocked sound. He bends, picking it up, staring at the work of folded paper. Smoothing out the creases, he looks at Mydei, clearly bewildered.

“Even here,” Mydei murmurs. “The stories can reach us even here.”

Another hand shoots forth from the dark, and Peucesta takes that one. Mydei’s librarians move like dancers, their blades whirling as they cut hand after hand, until they’re all standing ankle deep in paper. They are well accustomed to this, and they easily fend off the graspers. 

Light explodes from below them, flooding the lift. They emerge from the narrow shaft into a massive cavern, well lit by a tremendous number of gaslamps lining neatly organized boulevards. Here, there are barracks for the librarian-guards on duty, a number of small shops built into the rock itself, a tavern.

Perdikkas inhales deeply. “Antoine is making ratatouille,” he says, sheathing his blade.

Phainon stares at him, at Mydei. “There were—there were hands,” he says. “In the walls.”

“Graspers,” Ptolemy supplies.

Phainon continues as if he didn’t hear him. “There were hands in the walls and you’re talking about—about lunch?”

“Better to get a meal now than waste our supplies,” Perdikkas says cheerfully.

Leonnius claps Phainon on the shoulder. “Think of it as a celebration.”

“A celebration?”

“The graspers didn’t choke you to death on the way down. A good omen, no?”

Phainon chokes now as the lift finally reaches its end, grinding to a halt.

The librarians pull the doors open and spill out of the lift. Hephaestion and Leonnius hold the doors as Mydei turns to Phainon. “We can go back up. Your presence—my presence—isn’t necessary. They can find your book without us.” He expects Phainon to bend.

Instead, Phainon grips the hilt of his zweihander and sets his expression. “No. No, I want to be here.”

“Suit yourself,” Mydei says, stepping out of the lift.

Phainon darts forward to avoid being trapped.

They do take a quick meal at Antoine’s, where Peucesta works the room for information—new discoveries, migration patterns of the Library’s custodians, landslides from shelves collapsing. Once they’ve eaten their fill, Mydei herds them to the main gate, where Peucesta takes the lead. He navigates them through the narrow, winding pathway cut through the rock that takes them from the Library’s entrance into the Library proper. And when they step out of that narrow pathway, they stand aside so that Phainon can take in the expanse of it.

There is something charming about taking someone into the Library who has never been before, about watching wonder spill like ink across their face as they take in the sweeping vista inside the mountain, the bookshelves taller than the tallest buildings, the sparkling lake on the far side of the stacks, the blue-white light of the crystals glowing in the distant ceiling. Before them stretches a valley cut by rivers of bookshelves, twisting turns on cobbled streets lit by yet more gas lamps, a city of knowledge with paper houses. At the distant center of the twisting pathways grows a gargantuan tree, its red and white leaves dripping over a central clearing. Lanterns hang heavy from its boughs, casting the area in a faint glow.

“We’re beneath a mountain,” Phainon says, staring.

“The mountains are vast,” Mydei replies. His librarians echo his words, murmuring them softly.

Phainon turns to him, awestruck. “Are there any mountains as vast as this? This is—this is a whole new world.”

“So is every book.” Mydei shrugs. “Come, your book is far, and the Library large. We should move quickly while the crystals are still alight and the lamps burn.”

Phainon falls in step beside Mydei, and they make their way down a series of steep switchbacks, descending the cliff into the first of the stacks. Here, they try to keep the most popular books, the ones people seek often, but the Library has its own custodians, and they often reshelve what the librarians place here.

“How long have the six of you been together?” Phainon asks as they enter the stacks, craning his neck to look at the monolithic shelves curving toward the crystalline sky.

Once more, Peucesta takes point, striding ahead of them on quiet, nimble feet. Though most custodians are harmless unless provoked, no librarian wants to roll those dice, for when the custodians decide they have a bone to pick with you, they quite literally pick apart your bones. Best to avoid them.

“Since birth,” Hephaestion replies.

Perdikkas scoffs. “The rest of us, only for five years,” he says. “We weren’t all weaned on the same wet nurse.”

“Explains your limp wrists,” Hephaestion teases, flopping his hands at Perdikkas.

Knocking his hands aside, Perdikkas rolls his eyes. “These weak wrists have set more than your fair share of bones.”

“Five years is an impressive tenure, isn’t it?” Phainon asks, ignoring their squabbling.

Mydei inclines his head as Leonnius slows behind them, guarding their backs. “Librarians who survive a year tend to survive the longest, but few survive the first year. These are the best.” He gives the squabbling pair, who have managed to drag Ptolemy into their fight as a referee, a long look before turning his eyes toward the crystals far above them. “Though one might not know it.”

“I think their camaraderie suggests otherwise,” Phainon says, a faint smile curling his lips. “They must work well together.”

“Phenomenally.” Mydei returns his gaze to the shelves around them, skimming his eyes over the titles and authors and committing the unfamiliar ones to memory. “We should endeavor to find simple fights before we venture too deep into the Library.”

Phainon startles. “Why?”

“So they can adapt to the two of us.” Mydei makes a thoughtful sound. “Or, rather, so they can adapt to you. I’ve fought with them before. They can accommodate my own style easily enough. You will be a nuisance to them.”

“Thanks,” Phainon drawls. “I can just sit the fights out, you know.”

“And then you will die. Do you want to die, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae?”

Strangely enough, Phainon laughs. “I’m not particularly worried about living or dying if I can get my hands on this book.”

How strange indeed. “Do you not want to read it? Does it not have value to you beyond holding it?”

“What a complicated question that is,” Phainon says.

Mydei lifts a brow. “Why else does someone want a book if not to read it?” He makes an ugly face. “Or are you some kind of collector?”

“Oh, I wouldn’t dare.” Phainon holds up a surrendering hand. “The last thing I want is the Library’s returns agents coming after me.”

“Then you are a wise man, even if you didn’t prepare a will in advance of this expedition.” Mydei’s expression melts into one of mild amusement, and he allows a small quirk of his lips.

Phainon laughs, and this time, it’s a lovely sound, like so much poetry. “We all fall short of perfection, don’t we?”

“We do, indeed.”

It’s another hour before they reach the tree at the center of the bookshelves. All around it are tables, as if for some sort of party that was never celebrated. Though hundreds of years have passed since the Library’s discovery, the wood hasn’t rotted or aged, and no one has had the heart to tear them down, as if in deference to whoever came before.

Phainon runs his fingers along one table lifting the tips to his eyes.

“Did you expect dust?” Mydei asks.

Phainon ducks his head. “No, I… don’t know what I expected, I suppose. Maybe that they wouldn’t be real. None of this feels real. A tree beneath a crystalline sky, a distant lake, all beneath a mountain?”

“The mountains are vast,” Hephaestion says, and the others echo him. Mydei doesn’t; he is a cataloguer, and he doesn’t share his librarians’ superstitions. 

“Are they hollow?” Phainon asks wryly.

Leonnius smacks the back of his shoulder. “Where’s your sense of wonder?” He clambers over one of the tables, hopping onto the blue grass from which the gargantuan tree grows. It’s so big around that Mydei would need at least five copies of himself to wrap his arms around the trunk completely. A faint wind blows through the center of the books, ruffling hair and rustling through the branches—leaving a faint, chiming melody in its wake.

Startled, Phainon whips around.

“It’s the tree,” Ptolemy says.

Phainon turns his eyes upward, toward the leaves, like so many shaped and painted brass chimes.

“I guess he found his wonder,” Hephaestion says. “But even here, we shouldn’t linger.” They have yet to encounter any custodians, for which Mydei is grateful, but the longer they go without seeing one, the more on edge he and his librarians become. Even now, Hephaestion’s eyes dart to all the pathways that empty into this central area as though he expects something to appear in one of them. But all of them are thus concerned—with the exception of Phainon, who doesn’t have the sense or experience to know any better. “Phainon.”

Craning his neck around, Phainon looks at Hephaestion. “Hm?”

“This way,” Hephaestion says, hopping onto the blue grass, too. He beckons as Peucesta approaches the trunk of the tree, winks at Phainon, and then disappears into it.

Phainon reels back.

“And you haven’t even seen the other side of it,” Mydei says, amused.

Phainon stares at him, a wide-eyed puppy.

“Let’s go,” Leonnius calls from where he leans against the tree. “Standing around gawking is asking for death. Move.”

“But—” Mydei propels Phainon forward with a hand between his shoulder blades, cutting him off. He catches himself on a table and stumbles up to Leonnius and Hephaestion.

Hephaestion places a bracing hand on the tree trunk. “Like this,” he says, and then he steps through a crack in the trunk only visible from a very specific angle.

Gawking, Phainon swings his eyes from Mydei to Leonnius and back again as Ptolemy and Perdikkas cluster nearby, their hands on their sword hilts. They all shift uneasily on their feet, rocking with a disquieted battle readiness. 

“This is not a library,” Phainon says to Leonnius, and then he ducks into the trunk.

Leonnius lifts both brows at Mydei, and Mydei shrugs. “It’s not an uncommon reaction,” Mydei says. Leonnius’s brows climb higher. “I’m not defending him in particular,” Mydei snaps. “It’s not an uncommon reaction. You tripped on a root because you were too busy picking your jaw off the ground the first time.”

Now, Leonnius rolls his eyes. “Move,” he says.

Mydei urges Perdikkas and Ptolemy through first and then follows them.

They emerge into a forest of ivory ruins and golden trees, and he has the good sense not to stop dead in Leonnius’s path. He steps to the side before he swears.

“What?” Phainon asks.

The others are nodding.

“Had the same reaction,” Peucesta says to Mydei. To Phainon, he says, “The Marbled Grove shouldn’t connect to the Music Tree.”

They shouldn’t be anywhere near the Marbled Grove. The Marbled Grove—Room EN-492-6.73—is much, much deeper in the Library. They should be in Room HP-755-0.62.

“We should be in the Statue’s Ballroom,” Mydei says, flexing his fingers in his gauntlets. “No one told you this connection changed?”

Peucesta shook his head. “I would’ve gone a different way if I knew.”

“Wait,” Phainon says, holding up both hands. “Are you telling me—” He gestures at the cracked rock Leonnius has just peeled himself out of. “—doors, for a given value of door, don’t always lead to the same place here?”

They stare at him as though he’s stupid, but that’s unfair. He’s not a librarian, but this is why the right of discovery shouldn’t exist. Why it pains every librarian and cataloguer.

“Pieces of the Library have a tendency to move when no one’s looking directly at them,” Ptolemy finally says, offering up the explanation the others clearly don’t know how to give. All librarians tend to take this information for granted, even when they’re training new ones. Perhaps that’s one of the reasons so many die. “We should tell Antoine.”

Mydei frowns, crossing his arms. “We should go back.”

“You took my ink,” Phainon says.

“We can give it back to you,” Mydei reminds him. They are both silent, watching each other, tension running between them. It’s understandable that Phainon wants his book, but no book is so needed that it should cost the lives of Mydei’s librarians. The Marbled Grove is one of the worst rooms within the Library, and well most avoid it.

Hephaestion regards the path forward. “We’ve been here before,” he reminds Mydei. “As long as we take our time, it won’t be dangerous.” He reaches into his own knapsack, pulling out a teleslate. The librarians gather around it, making room for Mydei and Phainon as Hephaestion pulls up a digital map. “This is the nearest exit. It takes us to the Gilded Ravine, which is a pain in the ass but a far cry safer than here.”

“It’ll take three hours to get there,” Perdikkas says, scratching his chin. “If there’s a bone golem between here and there…”

“I’ll look.” Peucesta peels away, swinging nimbly onto the lowest branch of a nearby, bone-white tree. He climbs it on silent feet as Mydei returns his attention to the slate.

The path to the Ravine is long and arduous, the cliffs of the Grove descending into nothing but mist and cloud. Perhaps they should go back and try this again when the way is simpler.

“I can go back,” Leonnius volunteers. “Tell Antoine so no one else goes through the tree.”

But Phainon wears an alarmingly anxious expression, one that twists Mydei’s gut. His librarians are right: they’ve come this way before. They’ve dealt with the Grove in the past, and they’ve emerged unscathed. If they are slow and patient, they might lose a day or two, but they won’t need to delay Phainon from his book. A reader’s desire for a book shouldn’t be overlooked.

Mydei shakes his head. “No. If we’re going to spend three hours here, I want you with us. We’ll hang a tag on the tree so those who come after know the way has changed. Leonnius?”

He nods, shrugging off his pack and digging through it to find the long, white ribbon librarians use as a warning. “On it,” he says, turning back to the cracked rock they all emerged from.

Leaning away from the group, Mydei peers through the golden leaves for a glimpse of Peucesta. The man is at the top of a tree, clinging to a ruined marble wall and peering into the distance. He turns his attention to Perdikkas. “Do you have enough salves to get us through if we get burned half to death?”

“Half to death? No. But as long as we don’t eat too many attacks, we’ll be fine,” Perdikkas says, casting a long glance at Phainon.

“Door’s closed,” Leonnius calls out.

Every one of them looks up at him. He stands deep in the crack, shimmying with obvious discomfort, pressed between two large pieces of rough marble, his expression pinched.

“What do you mean?” Mydei asks.

“I mean,” Leonnius says, managing to free his torso. He braces his hands on the rock and pushes, pulling his waist and legs free of their tight confines. “I mean, the door’s closed.” He regards the rock with crossed arms. “Is this the usual entry point?”

Ptolemy shakes his head. “No, it’s not. We’re probably half a day east of that.”

“Well, shit,” Leonnius mutters, stuffing his tag back into his knapsack. “Looks like the Ravine’s the only choice, then.”

Mydei crosses one arm over his chest, resting the fingers of his other hand against his chin. The Library, for all it can move and change, isn’t sentient. It doesn’t think. It’s not malicious. But this feels deliberate, like it’s making these changes intentionally. Like it wants them to press forward into increased danger.

Peucesta drops out of his tree and returns to them. “No bone golems that I could see. A few stone guardians, but those aren’t much of a problem.”

“Then we continue,” Hephaestion says, tapping off his slate and tucking it back in his own knapsack. He looks at Mydei for confirmation.

Mydei is no librarian but he understands the Library in a way they don’t. It’s a cataloguers job to see how the rooms within the library fit together, to find safe paths through them for the librarians to take. From the Grove to the Ravine, and from there, they can access the Crescent Harbor and walk the strand to the Recital Chamber, where they’ll find Phainon’s book.

“We continue,” Mydei says at last.

They continue, Peucesta scouting ahead and Hephaestion leading the way. Occasionally, Peucesta drops back to check in with Hephaestion before bounding ahead once more, ensuring the way before them is safe for their passage. By the end of the first hour, everyone in the party, even Phainon, is on edge. By the end of the second, Mydei struggles to stave off his own mounting anxieties.

“Mydei,” Phainon says softly.

Mydei grunts in response, gauntleted fists hanging at his side, ready to be used. He’s tense with his anticipation, listening carefully to the silence. There is no birdsong in the Library, though there are paper birds that flutter by on occasion. Flying custodians roost in some rooms, but none call the Marbled Grove home.

“We haven’t seen any… what did you call them? Stone guardians?”

“We haven’t,” Mydei agrees.

For a moment, Phainon is quiet. “Did something else clear them out?”

Perdikkas, who is closest to them, rubs his thumb against his fingers, an old librarian gesture for warding off evil.

“That,” Mydei says, “is the reason we’re all so tense.” His lips press into a thin line. All around them, white ruins rise from mist. Shelves are carved deep into what looks like white marble, heavy laden with books. The only good thing about the Marbled Grove with its golden trees overhanging every pathway is that the shelves aren’t inclined to collapse under the weight of their books, reducing the concern for avalanches. He would take an avalanche over this unnatural quiet. “If there are no stone guardians lurking in the bone ruins—”

“Bone ruins?” Phainon hisses. “You said this was the Marbled Grove.”

“It is.”

“Bone ruins,” Phainon says again, emphatically.

Mydei shrugs. “The ruins were carved out of marbled bone, and sometimes pieces of those ruins come to life.”

“Bone golems,” Perdikkas says, rubbing his thumb over his fingers again.

Phainon glances from Perdikkas to Mydei. “And they’re dangerous?”

“Exceptionally,” Mydei says. He glances at Ptolemy, several paces ahead, beside Hephaestion. “Ptolemy lost his last team to a bone golem.”

Phainon’s expression tightens. “How many?”

“Seven dead. He was the only survivor.”

“Shit,” Phainon breathes. “Why do people even come here?”

“Why are you here?” Mydei asks, giving him a pointed look. “Why would anyone come to a library? Knowledge begets power, power is addicting, and men are addicts.”

Phainon is quiet for a moment before saying, softly, “Not all of us.”

Mydei laughs, but not unkindly. “You’re an optimist, then. How remarkably rare.”

They emerge from beneath a canopy of golden leaves to find a bridge stretching across a deep gorge filled with mist and swirling clouds. Peucesta waits for them beside the bridge, expression drawn.

“We have to cross it,” he says as the rest of them cluster around him.

“Real good place for an ambush,” Phainon observes, and Mydei makes a soft sound of agreement, impressed. A former reader to the emperor capable of drawing tactical conclusions surprises him.

Hephaestion pulls out his teleslate, tapping the screen. “There’s no good way around this gorge that doesn’t add twelve or more hours to our route.”

The trouble, of course, is that Phainon hasn’t put a timeline on his requisition, but the Library itself has one. Prolonged stays in the Library increase the odds of death. They either extend their time among the stacks, gambling with their lives, or they cross the bridge, gambling anyway.

“Better to just take the bridge,” Leonnius says.

Ptolemy nods. “The other routes around the bridge take us lower, through the mist layer. Visibility will diminish even more. The risk is greater.”

“Then we cross here,” Mydei says, “and hope our luck holds.” He gives Hephaestion a pointed look as the other man puts his teleslate away. Hephaestion draws his blade, and the others follow suit. Phainon, seeing their readiness, unsheathes his zweihander as well, his expression tight. Grim. Good. Mydei inclines his head toward Phainon. “In the worst case, leave most of the fighting to us.”

“Understood,” he says, and Mydei believes him. Phainon holds his zweihander with the casual familiarity of a man who has used it many, many times. A former reader for the emperor who knows his way around a blade. How extremely strange.

To his librarians, Mydei says, “Quietly. Carefully.”

They nod.

Once more, Peucesta takes point, Leonnius hangs behind them, and they begin across the bridge. Oppressive silence closes around them, punctuated only by the crunching of golden leaves beneath their feet. Tension reverberates through Mydei’s bones, growing with every step. They’re a third of the way across the bridge. Halfway. He is hyperaware of everything around him: his librarians’ movements and proximity, Phainon’s presence flanking him to the right, the strange wind that blows through the Grove, a whistling sound from above.

He looks up.

The bone golem crashes down onto them, onto Peucesta, splattering him across the bridge in a shower of blood and gore.

There is a moment of stunned silence, of perfect stillness as the golem remains crouched on the bridge. No one moves. Mydei can’t even breathe. He stares at the bloodstain that was once a person, his heart hammering in his chest but his mind keen with the knowledge that there is no time for grief.

Rising, the golem stands well over fifteen feet tall, an amalgamation of everything it has killed before them. Human skulls make up its torso, rib cages from other custodians its arms and thighs. A spiked skull on either shoulder serves as pauldrons. Spindly, grasping fingers extend from its every surface, pushing through gaps between other bones to reach for the closest librarians.

Mydei shoves Phainon back as Leonnius and Hephaestion leap forward with anguished cries; there’s no need to be silent anymore. They duck beneath the golem’s heavy fists, slicing away those smaller grasping hands, aiming their blades for the glowing blue core at the heart of the golem’s abdomen.

From the backline comes the crack of a pistol, Ptolemy’s clever eye taking aim at the golem. The bullet explodes through what might be the golem’s face, sending it teetering backwards. It wheels its arms wildly, catching its balance before it topples over, and brings two massive fists down on the surface of the bridge. Hephaestion only just dodges out of the way, flanked by Leonnius, who lunges beneath the golem’s guard, angling his blade at its stomach.

The golem swipes one hand to the side, and there’s no avoiding it. It slams Leonnius into the bridge’s railing with a sickening crack. Leonnius crumples to the ground. He does not get up.

Mydei lurches into motion to the sound of another gunshot. This one skims over the skulls protecting the golem’s ribcage, shattering one of them. Ptolemy curses. Instead of falling to the ground, the shards shoot in all directions, firing outward.

“Don’t let the shards hit you!” Mydei calls out, twisting away from the ones he can and knocking the others from the air.

Behind him, he hears more stone darts pinging against a blade—Phainon’s, he assumes, since Perdikkas carries only a dagger and Ptolemy is certainly being more careful with his aiming.

But though they dodge, there are far too many shards in the air, and they cut through space as though they have minds of their own. Beyond the golem, Hephaestion’s sword swings in graceful arcs, knocking many of the shards aside, but not all of them. One pierces deep into his shoulder, and Mydei lets out a cry of alarm.

Not Hephaestion. No, not Hephaestion, anyone but Hephaestion.

Abandoning his defense of Phainon, Ptolemy, and Perdikkas, he ducks beneath the golem’s fists, rushing up to Hephaestion. His gauntlets make him clumsy as he reaches for the shard, tearing it from Hephaestion’s flesh, knowing already that it’s too late.

Hephaestion grabs him by the throat, his eyes vacant when he looks up.

“Mydei!” The cry comes from someone behind him, but he doesn’t care which of them is shouting his name.

There are fixes for this. Strong men have overcome a bone golem’s control, and Hephaestion is a strong man, the strongest Mydei knows. But Hephaestion’s grip tightens around his throat, and Hephaestion readies his sword, and Hephaestion is going to kill him. His vision clouds at the edges, and he grips Hephaestion’s wrist, fighting with himself. Breaking free means breaking his oldest friend’s wrist, and he isn’t as strong as he needs to be.

A bullet explodes through Hephaestion’s head.

For just one moment, there’s clarity in Hephaestion’s eyes—clarity, and grief. Then his hand relaxes and he drops to the ground in a pool of blood, dead. Just like that, he’s dead.

And if Mydei doesn’t pull himself together, he’ll be dead, too.

He whirls around, horrified to see the bone golem crowding Phainon, Perdikkas, and Ptolemy back toward the start of the bridge, where a pair of stone guardians stand. Marble statues, as tall as a man but no more, wielding oversized great swords of impossibly hard gold, their faces have been worn away by time. Before Mydei can shout a warning, one lunges forward in an elegant, fencer’s thrust.

Gold bursts from Perdikkas’s chest, a long line of it.

This isn’t happening. This can’t be happening.

The guardian drags its blade upward, splitting Perdikkas in half from the chest up. Ptolemy whirls around, but his bullets are useless against stone guardians, who have no visible core.

They’re going to die here.

No. No, they will not die here.

With the bone golem distracted, Mydei rushes it. He leaps from the ground, grabbing a bone that runs across the breadth of its back and slams his gauntleted fist into the bones protecting it. Once, twice. They crack beneath him. He has limited time. If he shatters these bones, they will possess him as they did Hephaestion, and all of them truly will be dead.

Pulling back his elbow, he slams it forward, pulverizing bone and carving through to the golem’s core from behind. He grasps it in his fist as bone shards turn on him, ripping the glowing crystal from its home.

The golem crumbles into dust beneath him, and he drops to the ground to find Ptolemy aiming in his direction, horror in his eyes.

“Mydei,” Ptolemy whispers.

“Focus,” Mydei snaps. They have no time for despair. Phainon fights the twin guardians by himself, and Mydei can’t imagine he’s going to hold up well on his own.

“No, behind—”

Mydei whips around to find another stone guardian approaching with measured steps from the far end of the bridge. “Help Phainon,” he says, though there’s not much Ptolemy can do. Mydei leaps forward, ducking beneath the sweeping arc of the guardian’s blade, sliding across the stone bridge. He kicks one of its knees, and the creature shrieks, a loud and grating sound that momentarily stuns him. Its blade soars through the air toward his throat, and he is faced with the terrifying realization of his own impending death. Hubris catches up to everyone eventually.

A warm body collides with his, the force of it pushing him forward. The blade cuts above his head, making a sick, wet sound as it collides with someone else’s flesh.

Mydei thinks he might be sick, but he doesn’t waste Ptolemy’s sacrifice. He surges to his feet and grasps the guardian’s head in both hands. With a roar, he pulverizes stone, his gauntlets hissing as he triggers the pneumatic mechanisms that provide additional power to his grip.

The guardian drops, but Mydei doesn’t take time to pause. If he loses Phainon here, better for him to die, too. No cataloguer’s career survives the loss of a patron. Not like this.

He sprints back across the bridge, eyes fixed on the two guardians Phainon duels, refusing to look at the carnage around him. Refusing to acknowledge it. Pools of blood splash around his feet, but that blood belongs to other people, not his librarians. Not his friends. They are alive and well at Antoine’s, and this—this is a nightmare from which he’ll soon wake. 

Both guardians are engaged with Phainon, giving Mydei the ability to flank one. He grabs its forearm and yanks hard, putting all his momentum into his grapple to drive the creature backwards. It loses its footing, crashing to the ground on its back, and he pummels its head to powder.

Blade grates on stone, but he doesn’t look up from his macabre work to see Phainon dispatch the other guardian. He continues beating his gauntlets against the guardian until fingers brush over his shoulder.

Jerking around, he blindly drives his fist forward, and Phainon only just dodges it. Mydei is screaming.

He stops, panting, and finally sees the battlefield. There is nothing left of Peucesta. Leonnius lays at an impossible angle. Hephaestion, on his back, surrounded by blood. Ptolemy with his head shorn of, and Perdikkas, split in twain from the chest up.

“No,” he says, staring blankly into the distance. “No. This… this did not…”

It’s real. He knows it’s real. But he can’t accept that it’s real. He can’t. Any second now, Perdikkas will move, will rush over to Hephaestion or Leonnius, will apply a salve and a bandage even though no salve and no bandage can fix these mortal wounds. They will, all of them, get up, and then they will continue. They will… they will continue. They have to continue.

A hand curls around his elbow and hauls him up. He stumbles onto his feet, numb.

“We have to continue,” Phainon says. He is splattered in blood.

Mydei meets Phainon’s eyes. Hard. Unyielding. A man who has tasted bitterness but chooses joy. Phainon is familiar with this kind of death.

Swallowing, Mydei nods. “We… yes. We have to continue.” Not because Phainon’s book is so important but because all the noise will draw more custodians. They can’t remain here.

Still numb, Mydei steps forward, now fixing his gaze on Hephaestion. Hephaestion with a hole in his head, eyes empty. Mydei closes his own eyes when he rolls Hephaestion over, stripping his knapsack from his back. They need his teleslate. Mydei knows the rooms, he knows how they connect, but Hephaestion’s maps will help them orient themselves if they stumble into another mistake.

And he needs to take some part of his oldest, closest, best friend with him.

“We continue,” he says to himself, fixing his gaze on the far end of the bridge.

Phainon is at his side, keeping pace with him, but he is blind to everything but the end of the bridge. To the small cottage beyond it. To the door that will take them to the Gilded Ravine. Close. It was so close. It was so close, and his librarians are dead. His friends are dead.

Through the cottage door, they continue.
