The door to the small cottage doesn’t open into a home. It takes them to a deep gulch of brown stone that serves as shelves. Above them, trees with green leaves shade them from the blue-white light of the crystals far overhead. A shallow stream runs underfoot. Mydei stands in the water, letting it wash his boots clean of all the blood.

Phainon joins him.

When the door closes behind them, it disappears, becoming one with the rock. There is nowhere to go but forward. Mydei doesn’t know how to go forward. Librarians die. He has lost librarians, many times, but never Hephaestion. Never these men, who have been his friends for five years.

“Men like them aren’t supposed to die,” he says.

“The world is unkind to good men,” Phainon replies, bending and dipping his hands into the water. He cups them together and lifts them to his face, washing away the blood of Mydei’s friends. Perdikkas’s, probably.

“You didn’t know them.” Mydei tips back his head, staring at the green-leaved canopy far above them, light glinting off the mirrors growing from the walls of the ravine.

Phainon drops his hands, letting the water wash away the blood on them. “No. I didn’t. And I’m poorer for it.” He rises. “Is it safer here?”

“That depends.” Mydei gestures to the mirrors. “They will tempt you, each with a different vision of a past or future you could have had if only you’d done something just a bit differently.” Phainon mutters an oath. “Gaze too long, and the mirror-soul within will drag you into the glass and trap you there.”

With a sound of protest, Phainon says, “This is supposed to be a library.”

“All the books in the universe, Phainon,” Mydei replies wearily. “All the books in the universe come to the Library. There must be a price, a hardship, for getting one’s hands on that knowledge.” He tips his head toward Phainon, studying him. “Is your book worth this price?”

Phainon regards the water streaming around his feet but says nothing. He doesn’t need to. All men are the same. They would sacrifice everything for the power of the knowledge they seek. Mydei’s friends are nothing to him. Mydei’s friends are—

A tear drips from Phainon’s face. It hits the surface of the stream, and the water ripples around them. Another tear falls. Another. Still silent, Phainon lifts a hand to his face, covering his eyes.

Mydei’s friends are dead, and Phainon weeps. It’s more than others have done for the librarians who died for them. It’s more than Mydei expected of him.

“We shouldn’t remain here,” Mydei says. “It’s dangerous to stay still.” He walks forward, wading through the water.

Phainon follows him.

“The custodians here are usually benign,” Mydei says, needing to talk, needing to do something to keep his mind off his friends. “They are sprites, no bigger than your hand, and they have a subtle glow about them. Often green, but sometimes blue or yellow. You’ll see them in the trees.” He doesn’t bother looking either for the sprites or at Phainon. “They polish the mirrors, and they don’t like when you smudge the glass, so keep your hands to yourself.”

“Eyes down, hands to myself,” Phainon says.

“Eyes up,” Mydei corrects. “Glancing at the mirrors is fine. Don’t stare. But stay sharp. Custodians from other rooms sometimes wander into the Ravine.”

Phainon makes a quiet sound of acknowledgement, and they walk in silence, following the little stream that runs over their feet. It deepens, the gulch widens, and Mydei pulls to one side, keeping to the shallows. He wraps his fingers around Hephaestion’s knapsack, clinging to the strap, but he doesn’t stop to remove the teleslate. The Ravine is familiar enough to him, a common crossroads to many other rooms.

“Mydei,” Phainon ventures after some thirty minutes of silence, of them following the stream through the still-narrow gulch.

“What?”

“Have you ever looked into any of these mirrors?”

Mydei snorts. “No.”

“Why not?”

“The future is something we create for ourselves, and there’s no point in regretting the past,” Mydei says. Now, though, he isn’t so sure. He glances at a mirror growing from the rock at an odd angle for just long enough to catch sight of Hephaestion’s face, heavy with a graying beard.

He looks away, swallowing hard.

“You have no regrets?” Phainon asks. And then, quickly, he adds, “No, I’m sorry. Please, don’t answer that. That was—I didn’t mean—Fuck.”

Mydei presses a hand to his chest, hollow and empty. “Until today, I had no regrets.”

“Now you have one,” Phainon says, and he means himself.

Mydei shakes his head. “No. I have five.” Phainon didn’t kill his librarians. A bone golem’s ambush did.

He expects Phainon to apologize, to offer some empty platitude or sorry condolence. Instead, Phainon says, “I think I’d lose myself in these mirrors too easily.”

One of Mydei’s brows lift. “Do you have so many regrets?”

“Every person I’ve failed,” Phainon says, and Mydei stops walking, turning to face him. Anger burns through him. This is Phainon’s attempt at an apology, and it makes fury ache in his bones. “Not just your friends. There are…” He closes his eyes, spreading his arms to either side, just a bit, enough to make himself vulnerable, and Mydei considers ripping out his heart. “There are so many people who want something better for themselves.” He opens his eyes, and they are sad. “And some of them want things at odds with the wants of others.”

Some of Mydei’s anger subsides, and he clicks his tongue with disdain. “You can’t make everyone happy.”

“No,” Phainon agrees. “You can’t. But I… I would like to do the most good. And to make good where I have done harm.”

Mydei’s mouth pulls in a half-hearted sneer. He is angry, yes, but he the loss is to fresh for him to cling to it. Maybe tomorrow, he will stoke his fury. “Tell me: can readers bring back the dead?”

Phainon looks away. “No,” he says softly.

“You could have read something in combat, no? Provided us with defenses. Shields. Weakened the golem.”

Phainon’s eyes close. “I don’t have combat readings.”

“But you wield a zweihander,” Mydei says, accusatory.

“It’s… complicated.”

Mydei snarls softly. “Make it less complicated. We’re stuck in the Library, alone with each other, dependent on each other. Your readings could mean the difference between life and death.”

Phainon holds up both hands, opening his eyes to meet Mydei’s gaze. “My specialty was poetry—poetry about nature.”

“You lied to me.”

He shakes his head. “No, I—I—”

“A lie of omission is still a lie.” There’s a flash of something in Phainon’s eyes, something like fear, and Mydei pounces on it. “You let me bring you here thinking you would be useful in combat, and instead all you can do is—is what? Make pretty flowers grow out of the ground? Could you not have used vines to restrain the golem? Could you not have blinded it with light?”

“And caused your friends to trip on the vines? To blind them as well?” Phainon asks, though he is soft, lacking the fiery accusation heavy-laden in Mydei’s own tone. “Such recitations almost always backfire.”

“You could have memorized something,” Mydei says.

Pain filters across Phainon’s face. “And I wish I had. I wish I had been able to do something, anything, to have affected a different outcome. Do you want me to beg your forgiveness?” He drops down, splashing into the water, and spreads his arms wide. “Do you want me on my knees?”

Mydei recoils. “No, I—”

“Had I prepared better, maybe they would still be alive,” Phainon continues. “Had I brought poems about war, about death, about conflict and turmoil, perhaps a stanza, a line, might have saved even one of them, and I will live with that for the rest of my life.” Anguish lines his face, pours into his every word. “I will live with their deaths, Mydei, and it will haunt me.” The genuine grief catches Mydei by surprise. Phainon didn’t know his friends, but he is genuinely pained by their deaths, and that assuages his own grief, at least to a small degree.

“Get up,” he says, turning away. “We don’t have time for this.” Water drips from Phainon’s legs as he rises. “Stay close—and don’t look in the mirrors.”

“Of course,” Phainon murmurs.

In silence, they continue walking, following the expanding gulch and the deepening stream. Minutes crawl by, and Mydei is content with the quiet, content to listen to the sighing, impossible wind—there should be no wind beneath the mountain, but he has long wondered if the Library is truly contained beneath the mountain it’s built on. Maybe that first room, but the others? Perhaps not. Perhaps the Library is a tangled labyrinth of worlds, distorted by the metaphysical weight of the books it contains. Maybe there are universes out there where his friends yet live. Rather than bringing relief, that thought is a cruelty.

The wind howls mournfully, soft and gentle, carrying with it muffled sounds, faint callings of his own name. Mydei’s fingers curl into loose fists. “What do you hear on the wind?” he asks.

“Names,” Phainon says. “The names of the dead. They’re coming from the mirrors, aren’t they?”

Mydei makes a soft sound of acknowledgement. “The mirror-souls want us to look at them.”

“I won’t.” Phainon’s voice is tight.

Mydei keeps his gaze on the path ahead of them, but the wind’s murmurs grow louder. Ptolemy calls his name, cajoling him to come to a fragment of glass, to peer inside, to see the fascinating book he’s discovered. Mydei turns away from the mirror only to catch sight of Leonnius racing his brothers in another. Leonnius waves to him, a fierce grin on his face, and Mydei almost stumbles. Almost steps closer.

Onward. He presses onward, Phainon at his back, as Perdikkas snaps at him to stop complaining about the pain of his stitches. As Peucesta plays a simple song on guitar, a song his other friends join in on, raising their voices in butchered yet beautiful harmony. As his mother calls out, “My darling, my darling, do not weep, I’m here.”

His mother, his beautiful mother. He can’t help but look toward her, toward where she reaches from a nearby mirror, leaning out of the frame. He knows it’s the mirror-soul gowned in his own memories, but there she is in white lace and ivory linen, a feathered hat pinned to her copper hair. Grief lines her face, and she holds out her gloved hands to him.

“My darling, my darling,” she implores. “Let me hold you, my darling.”

She isn’t real, and her comfort is a farce. Mydei turns away from his mother and into Phainon’s restraining hand. Worry creases Phainon’s brow, and Mydei, embarrassed, refuses to meet his eyes.

“I’m fine,” he says.

Phainon releases him. “Are you?”

No. “Yes. The mirrors are persistent today. I can manage.”

Phainon doesn’t look like he believes Mydei, eyes narrowed, lips pressed in a thin line, jaw set. “I can take the lead.”

“You don’t know where we’re going.”

He looks over Mydei’s shoulder, to the basin beyond them. “The other side of this clearing, I’d wager.” His tone is wry.

With a quiet laugh, Mydei steps back. “And then? Where do we go from there?” he asks, but he’s teasing rather than biting.

Phainon offers a shy smile, and Mydei can’t help but think it’s a handsome one. Those bright eyes, those full lips. Phainon himself is handsome, not just his smile, and Mydei wishes they’d met some other way, that Phainon hadn’t come to him in search of a book buried in the stacks.

“Be wary in the basin,” Mydei says, turning toward the mouth of the gulch and stepping out of its shade. Blue-white crystal light filters down to them, bright and almost painful. He blinks as his eyes adjust, flexing his fingers.

Phainon draws his blade. “Even though there aren’t any mirrors?’

“There are,” Mydei corrects, leading the way. He steps out of the shallows onto springy grass that glitters faintly, the gilded edges catching the crystalline light from above. “They’re just hidden beneath the grass and the moss. Keep your eyes forward.” Across from the basin, the forest grows wild and dense, the trees a normal green though they, too, are gilded. Another hour down the overgrown path is a well, and that will take them to the Crescent Harbor. They’re close. They’re so close.

But the basin is wide, devoid of trees or cover of any kind, and the space above them is just as dangerous as the ground beneath. Sprites flit overhead, zipping about only to pause, hanging in the air as though watching him. Maybe they are.

He walks carefully, feeling out the ground to make sure he doesn’t trip on a moss-covered mirror. Every step is calculated, slow, and Phainon keeps pace behind him.

“Do you want to talk about what you saw in the mirror?” Phainon asks.

“No,” Mydei says, scanning the basin. He puts a foot down, and it slides across moss and grass, and he swears, wheeling backwards.

Phainon catches him beneath his arms, but the weight of him sends Phainon stumbling backwards, too. They land not on grassy earth but the cool, hard surface of a mirror, and Mydei swears, lurching forward.

He’s not fast enough.

Ribbons of black, like so many arms, shoot out of the mirror—the mirror-soul, furious at being disturbed. It grabs at him, at Phainon, dragging them backwards, pulling them toward the rippling, silvery surface of its body. Phainon shoves Mydei away, and Mydei staggers, catching himself quickly before whipping around and grabbing Phainon’s hand.

“Let go!” Phainon says, clutching the edge of the mirror. His legs have already been pulled inside. He swims up to his waist in a pool of reflective glass.

Mydei grips Phainon harder, gritting his teeth, pulling against the mirror-soul. Not again. He won’t lose someone again, not even Phainon, not even this man he barely knows who went to his knees to beg Mydei’s forgiveness for the Library’s crime.

Bracing one foot against the edge of the mirror, Mydei pulls. Phainon levers himself against the mirror’s frame at the same time, but it’s not enough. The mirror-soul is strong, stronger than them. Phainon, with a cry, loses his grip on the frame and plunges into the mirror.

Mydei, refusing to let go, falls with him.

They hit the ground of a grassy meadow, surrounded by a ring of mirrors, and as they stagger to their feet, Phainon clutching his head with one hand, a mirror as tall as a lamppost and twice as wide as it is tall floats before them.

“Fuck,” Mydei says, grabbing Phainon by the shoulder and yanking him around.

Phainon drops his hand from his head, groans, and reaches for his zweihander, drawing it. “Are we… inside the mirror? Is there a mirror inside the mirror? Is—”

A man emerges from the mirror, clothed in suit that is crisp and blue, his hair tidy beneath his hat, his shoes polished to a shine. He is impeccable, untouchable, irreproachable, and Mydei takes an involuntary step forward.

Phainon catches him. “Who is that?”

“You can see him?” Mydei swallows hard.

“I was so proud of you, boy,” Eurypon says, his gentle voice a terrible thing, a debilitating verbal strike. Mydei staggers.

This isn’t real. The mirror-soul’s artifice isn’t real, but Eurypon looks real, sounds real. Tobacco and cognac hang around him in a cloud. He smells real, smells like home. Like family.

“What have you done, boy?”

Fingers squeeze Mydei’s elbow. “Mydei?” Phainon asks.

Eurypon’s expression isn’t cruel, but rather is one of profound, profound disappointment. “What have you done?” Eurypon asks again, forlorn, the question devastating. “Chief Cataloguer at twenty-two, and you’ve thrown it all away.” He has. He’s destroyed his career. His impeccable reputation. He’ll lose his position, and his family will suffer for it.

“Mydei?” Phainon asks again, worry in his voice. “What is this? What’s going on?”

Mydei’s jaw works but he can’t force out words, can’t look away from the image of his father so disappointed in him. Can’t look away from the image of his own face reflected in Eurypon’s, their features so similar. His father’s face, but his mother’s coloring.

“You failed your librarians,” Eurypon says. “You let them die. What kind of Chief Cataloguer lets his librarians die?”

“It wasn’t like that,” Mydei protests. “I didn’t—”

Phainon releases him, swings his blade forward, and stabs into Eurypon’s heart. Eurypon shatters into shards of glass, and a terrible shriek comes from the mirror behind him. Mydei should look away, but he can’t; as Eurypon fades, Mydei’s gaze catches on his own reflection, on him and his friends in a drawing room, port in their hands, laughing and gray. Silver in their beards, on their temples. Deep laugh lines in their faces, all of them thicker around the middle than any librarian should be.

He failed them.

He failed his family.

When they escape the Library, his father will disinherit him. No son of Eurypon’s will bring such disgrace as this to the family name, not after everything else Eurypon has endured. Eurypon, the wastrel son of a peer who gambled away all his memory, and foreign Gorgo the rich merchant’s daughter who saved him and his estate. No one wanted anything to do with either of them until Mydei ascended to his position as Chief Cataloguer, and now—now he will be stripped of that position, his mother will lose her place in society, his father will be cast out, and his friends are dead.

He should be dead.

And the worst of this is that the mirror-soul isn’t reflecting what might be, it’s showing him what will be. He has lost his father’s regard, his mother’s happiness, and all of his friends. There is nothing left for him, no path forward. The Library will kill him and Phainon both, anyway. Fighting against it will prolong his suffering. Better to die here alongside his friends, another of the Library’s countless victims. That will spare his family the shame of his failure.

On his knees, he picks up one of those shards of glass.

He is careful in his handling of the glass, holding it delicately in his gauntlet’s fingers as he brings it to his throat. The sharp edge presses into his skin.

Someone calls his name, as though from a great distance.

In the mirror, he and his friends are laughing. His mother is crying. His father is turning away from him. He has nothing. He is nothing. He—

The mirror shatters, a blade driven through it. Beneath the falling pieces of glass is a roiling black mass, and Phainon drives his blade deeper into it, piercing through the glowing blue core of the mirror-soul.

Around them, the world flickers. Cracks.

There’s a sharp piece of glass against his throat.

Mydei drops it, rocking to his feet and staggering back a step. There is only grass beneath his feet. They’re back in the basin, an empty frame on the ground in front of them. Phainon clutches his zweihander in both hands, holding it at the ready, panting. He looks back, looks over his shoulder.

“You’re awake,” he says with obvious relief.

Staring at Phainon, his own hand to his throat, Mydei swallows down his rising gorge. “You—you saved my life. How?”

Phainon lowers his blade, sheathing it as he tuns to Mydei. “I overestimated the mirrors. It didn’t show me anything I don’t already know about myself.” Bitterness and joy.

“Its promises of the future,” Mydei ventures.

There’s a strange look on Phainon’s face. “What it offered couldn’t entice me.” He reaches out, taking Mydei’s elbow in his hand, comforting. Mydei doesn’t deserve— “I saw your friends, too,” he says softly. “Your mother. Your father.”

Mortified, Mydei looks away.

“This wasn’t your fault, and anyone who blames you is a fool,” Phainon says. “If it eases your conscience, you should blame me.”

He should blame Phainon. But he doesn’t. “You don’t know the Library like we do. Even if we hadn’t ventured out on this expedition, another one would have gotten them.” He lifts his face. “Librarians don’t retire. We all know that.” He shudders once, a moment of weakness. “This way.” Removing himself from Phainon’s touch takes more effort than it should.

He leads the way to the forest, and Phainon follows.

Blue light purples as they arrive in the Crescent Harbor, the far above crystals dimming for the Library’s simulated night. They emerge from an archway in the center of the Harbor, sea salt filling Mydei’s nose. There are no people here, only the remains of a seaside town long abandoned. Down the sloping streets, waves glimmer on the horizon in what remains of the crystals’ light. Fifty years ago, a librarian attempted to sail from the Crescent Harbor, postulating that this body of water was the same on as in the first room. No one ever saw her again.

“What awaits us here?” Phainon asks.

“Shadows,” Mydei sighs. “Come, we’ll find a place to sleep.”

Phainon doesn’t ask if it’s safe, and Mydei doesn’t lie to him.

There are places in the Harbor that are safer than others, and though one such safe place is their destination, Mydei leads Phainon to the city center first. There stands a massive fountain. Strange creatures with heads like lions and bodies like beetles stand rampant, faintly glowing streams of water arching from their open mouths into the pool at their feet.

“Another door?” Phainon asks.

Mydei shakes his head. “Drink,” he says, cupping his hands in the water and bringing it to his face. All his physical exhaustion melts away. The thirst and faint hunger gnawing at his belly fade, too, replaced by fullness and satiation.

After watching Mydei, Phainon drinks, too, and he makes a soft sound of wonder.

“There are a handful of fountains throughout the Library like this one,” Mydei says. “Our routes are based on their locations. They’ll revitalize you, nourish you, and keep you alive if you have nothing else. But since the doors are unreliable, betting on their presence is never wise.”

“Hence the supplies.”

“Hence the supplies.” Mydei sighs, closing his eyes. Not even the fountains can replace sleep. “This way.”

Their footsteps are quiet even on the city’s cobbled streets, both of them stepping lightly. Mydei squints through the darkness, though he has this route memorized, turning and turning and turning until they come to a home tucked against the city’s outer wall. Like all the other buildings in the city, its outside wall is carved with shelves and lined with books. Phainon runs his fingers along the spines on one shelf as Mydei opens the door for them both.

Darkness crowds them inside the small, two-story home, but Mydei doesn’t go into his pack for a light. Instead, after shutting and barring the door, he reaches out blindly. “Phainon?”

“Here.”

His hand presses against Phainon’s chest, traveling across it to his shoulder and then following the line of his arm. He takes Phainon by the wrist. “This way. There are stairs.” They climb them to a room at the back of the house where there are no windows. Mydei bars this door, too, with a plank left behind by another librarian.

Phainon doesn’t ask if barring the doors will actually help, and Mydei doesn’t lie to him.

“There’s a bed somewhere in here,” Mydei says, shuffling through the room until his legs bump the frame. He grunts. “Found it.”

A hand grazes his back in the darkness, and his skin prickles with awareness as Phainon steps around him. “Are there springs under the mattress?”

“Wood boards.” Mydei eases onto his side of the bed, finally allowing himself to relax somewhat. His muscles no longer ache, and though he could keep walking now that they’ve drunk from the fountain, he wants nothing more than to press his face into the dank pillow and sleep. He is wrung dry, empty, carved out, hollow.

Phainon’s weight dips the mattress as he collapses onto it, groaning quietly.

“Sleep with your sword,” Mydei says even as he removes his gauntlets. His parrying dagger comes out of its sheath, and he slides it under the pillow, within easy reach. “Even shadows have to come through the doors.” He allows himself a mirthless laugh. “A small mercy.”

“The smallest of mercies,” Phainon agrees, which makes Mydei laugh again.

He wants to throw back his head and howl with laughter, wants to laugh until his sides hurt. Instead, he sets his gauntlets on the floor and lays himself across his tiny bed. It’s too short for him and the space afforded him so minimal he knows he’ll sleep poorly for fear of rolling off it in the night, but it’s still a bed, and in a room safer than many of the others.

As he settles on his back, he becomes painfully aware of the sound of his breath, of the sound of Phainon’s, of their proximity. With his librarians, they’d pile into this room, fight for who alone got the bed, and then the rest of them would take the floor. But Phainon fell in bed beside him without hesitation.

There’s a comfort in being so close to someone living. A reminder that he isn’t dead, either, perhaps.

“How long have you been Chief Cataloguer?” Phainon asks.

Mydei turns his head toward his voice. “A decade, maybe,” Mydei says, too tired to do the math. “Why?”

“How does one get the position? Are you elected into it?”

“No.” Mydei rolls to his side, facing Phainon in the darkness. This deep into the house, there’s no light. He can’t see any of Phainon’s face, and he wonders if Phainon is looking in his direction. “You earn it by knowing where books are and how to get to them efficiently. I started memorizing books and their associated rooms as a child. It was a fascination of mine. When I finished school and came to the Library, I already knew considerably more than most other cataloguers.”

Phainon chuckles. “A meteoric rise.”

“Something like that.”

“How fitting for you.”

Mydei doesn’t know what to make of that. “And you? How were you discovered as a reader?”

“The usual way. Read something out loud to a sweetheart, made flowers bloom. Sparkles and magic.”

“How fantastical for her,” Mydei drawls.

“Him,” Phainon says.

Mydei startles, surprised.

“Does it bother you?” Phainon asks. “I can sleep on the floor if it does.”

“It would be hypocritical for me to be bothered,” Mydei replies. How strange, the way the darkness makes men honest. He’s long guarded his own preferences lest someone use them against him. People still try. Men, women. Everyone wants the knowledge the Chief Cataloguer can access, and plenty have tried to seduce power from him.

Phainon makes a soft sound, one of quiet acknowledgement. “Was it Hephaestion?” he asks.

What profound insight. “He doesn’t share our inclinations,” Mydei says. “Or, rather, he didn’t. He wasn’t much interested in any inclination, truth be told. The Library owned his heart.”

The mattress dips as Phainon rolls, and Mydei becomes very aware of the fact that he doesn’t know how close Phainon is to him in the darkness. “That must have been difficult.”

“It… was.” Mydei closes his eyes against the burn of tears.

“I’m sorry,” Phainon says, his hand brushing over Mydei’s arm and settling on his shoulder.

Mydei doesn’t acknowledge the apology, too busy fighting back his tears, struggling against his own grief. He shakes, and Phainon shifts closer to him. Slowly, haltingly, Phainon gathers him close, until Mydei’s forehead rests against the hollow of Phainon’s throat, until Phainon’s arms come around him, but still he doesn’t cry. Won’t cry. Grieving means acknowledging that they’re gone, and if he gives into grief while they’re still in the stacks, they won’t make it out. There’s still a chance that they’ll make it out.

Warm lips touch the top of his head, a comforting kiss.

Mydei, pressing his hands to Phainon’s chest, tips back his head and takes those lips with his own. Instead of pulling away, Phainon slips one hand around the nape of Mydei’s neck, the other around the small of his back, and draws him closer still.

The kiss is chaste. Sweet. Their lips cling in the darkness as they sigh against each other’s mouths. Mydei’s fingers curl around the leather of Phainon’s armor, as though Phainon might, at any moment, simply disappear. As though Phainon died in the Marbled Grove, too. He couldn’t bear that. Couldn’t bear to be alone, and he clings desperately to Phainon as they tip their faces to come together in another kiss, a hungrier kiss.

Desire kindles low in Mydei’s abdomen, a pleasant and tingling heat that washes through him. It charges him with a bubbling effervescence, a strange sense of life. They lost his librarians in the Grove, but they survived. They’re alive. They’re alive.

He presses into Phainon’s body, surging against him, his kiss turning hungry. Phainon’s nails rake lightly across his scalp, and he shudders, parting his lips, flicking his tongue against Phainon’s mouth. Phainon groans, fisting the fabric of Mydei’s shirt, pulling at it not to urge Mydei away but as though he needs some kind of outlet for his own mounting desire.

The wet heat of Phainon’s tongue slides against Mydei’s, and Mydei’s hands yank at the heavy leather of Phainon’s trench coat. It needs to come off, he needs skin, he needs Phainon’s tongue in his mouth and Phainon’s hands on his body to feel even more alive. He needs—

Phainon draws back abruptly, catching Mydei’s wrists in his hands. “Is this a good idea?” he asks, panting.

“No,” Mydei says, pressing his mouth against Phainon’s again. Phainon doesn’t respond to the kiss. He leans away from Mydei but doesn’t go too far. Mydei feels the shake of his head against the pillow.

“Hey, we… we shouldn’t. We—I—” He groans, resting his forehead against Mydei’s. He releases his grip on Mydei’s clothes, cupping Mydei’s jaw and rubbing his thumb over the curve of Mydei’s cheek, a shockingly intimate gesture from a man rebuffing a potential lover. “Not here.”

So, Phainon will take his book and Mydei will never see him again. It’s better that way. He knows it is. The rejection still stings.

“Not here,” he says, withdrawing and rolling over, putting his back to Phainon.

“Mydei…”

He doesn’t say anything. Doesn’t justify himself or demand justifications from Phainon. Phainon’s right. They shouldn’t. Not here, where danger still lurks, where the distraction of sex could kill them. Feeling alive isn’t worth the risk.

There’s still a chance they’ll make it out.

“Good night, Mydei,” Phainon says, and he rolls over, too.

Mydei slips his hand beneath his pillow, wraps his fingers around the hilt of his dagger, and tries to sleep.

They don’t rise with the dawn, as the dawn can’t reach them, but they rise alive and well come morning. Mydei slept poorly, but he slept, and sleep combined with the fountain’s boons have him refreshed enough. He doesn’t ask after Phainon’s health, embarrassment over last night lingering too heavily around him. He barely looks at Phainon at all.

Once they’re ready, they venture out, returning to the fountain for a morning’s meal of crisp, clean, and slightly sweet water. From there, Mydei takes Phainon to the shore, where the strand, a narrow strip of land visible no matter the tide, leads them a mile into the water. Their pace is brisk; it takes only fifteen minutes to reach the towering sentinel stones at the end of the strand, two monolithic pillars of rough-hewn rock.

Between the stones, the air shimmers, revealing a glimpse of the Recital Chamber beyond it: row after row of seats leading up to a distant stage. Along the walls, wooden shelves filled with books. Instruments lean against the shelves and rest in the seats, all ready to be played by anyone who might step into the room.

“Don’t touch the instruments,” Mydei warns Phainon as he reaches out, drawing his fingers through the strange, liminal space that demarcates the two rooms. The sea salt air is cold, biting. The Recital Chamber is warmer by far. “There will be custodians in the audience, a mix of them from various rooms. They’re never aggressive, not here, and you should ignore them.”

Phainon nods. “Understood. Ignore the monsters. Leave the instruments alone. Anything else?”

“No.” Mydei exhales, long and slow. “Let’s finish this.”

“And then we can go home,” Phainon says quietly.

“And then we can go home,” Mydei echoes. He steps forward, passing between the stone monoliths and crossing from the sand of the strand to the carpeted floor of the Recital Chamber. It is better occupied than he expected, cadres of custodians turning toward him as he enters. He makes space for Phainon, who enters behind him and makes a quiet noise of surprise.

Phainon leans toward him. “Do the custodians… enjoy a show?” Phainon asks, his voice low.

“I’ve never seen so many here,” Mydei replies, which isn’t, perhaps, an answer. Phainon reaches for his zweihander, and Mydei catches his wrist. “Don’t.” He frowns, tipping his head to one side. “Do you hear that?”

There’s a faint, pizzicato plucking, the strings of a harp, perhaps, tremoring with music.

A strange dread curls in Mydei’s stomach. The Recital Chamber is largely harmless, except when someone plays an instrument. The custodians never do. Most of them don’t even have hands.

“The music,” Mydei says, starting forward, his eyes fixed on the navy curtains blocking the view of the stage. “We need to stop that music.”

“Music?” Phainon asks.

Light flashes, brilliant in the dimly lit Recital Chamber, a spotlight illuminating the stage. The curtains peel back as Mydei continues forward, his dread deepening. Instruments have been arranged on the stage, a full orchestra of them, all in a semi-circle around a lectern. The lectern isn’t for a conductor. It faces the audience as though waiting for someone to stand behind it, to face the crowd, to recite something.

The music swells, violins and violas floating in the air, cellos and basses leaning against non-existent shoulders. Their bows pull across their strings, guided by invisible hands. There is a weight to this music as warm brass fills the air, too, offering a harmony to the string instruments’ melodies. Mydei staggers, catching himself on the arm of an occupied aisle seat.

The custodian seated there, some strange, headless statue, its glowing blue core floating where its head should be, turns its body toward him. It makes a low groaning noise, something like a question, and then it laughs, ragged and grating.

It’s laughing at him, but its laughter can’t drown out the music. Louder. Louder. The melody grows and grows until the lyrical notes drive like spikes into his ears. He’s on his knees, his hands clasped over his ears. There’s a pounding in his head. His heartbeat hammers erratically in his chest. He can’t catch his breath, and his vision swims. Nausea churns in his stomach.

A warm hand presses against his back. Phainon’s hand.

Phainon.

He has to kill Phainon. No. No, that’s not his thought. That’s not—but Phainon killed his friends, his librarians. Phainon’s request for The Lamb and the Sinner is the reason they’re dead, is the reason his reputation will be destroyed when they return, is the reason for his mother’s unhappiness and his father’s disdainful disappointment. Phainon is the reason.

Phainon has to die.

He has to kill Phainon.

How clear the truth is. Someone—the responsible party—has to pay for all these cruelties. Phainon is responsible. It has to be Phainon.

Mydei drops one hand to the sloping floor, finds his balance, and then kicks backward, knocking Phainon’s legs out from under him.

With a shocked cry, Phainon hits the ground. In the time it takes for him to fall, Mydei gains his feet. He’s on top of Phainon a second later.

Drums pound. Trumpets blare a triumphant melody, a victor’s march.

He reaches out, reaches down. Wraps his hands around Phainon’s throat before Phainon can recover from having the wind knocked out of him. The pointed tips of his gauntleted fingers gouge into Phainon’s neck. His thumbs prick the underside of Phainon’s chin.

Phainon has to die. Has to pay in blood or gasping breaths for the pain he’s caused, for the destruction he’s wrought.

He squeezes harder. Beneath him, Phainon’s eyes are wide, his lips parted, but there is no terror in his face.

“What—what are you—?” Phainon chokes, wheezing. Gasping for air. His desperate breaths are a beautiful harmonic line to the melody sweeping through the Chamber.

Mydei leans over him, pressing harder on his throat. His fingers curl, digging deeper into flesh, piercing it until blood drips along gold. “Six lives,” Mydei hisses. “You owe me six lives.”

This close, Mydei can see Phainon’s pupils constrict with his terror.

And then Phainon’s palm hits his chin, snapping his head back. His teeth crack together, a sharp, strange punctuation in the melody flowing around him. Stunned, Mydei stares at the ceiling above him only to find himself on his back and Phainon running toward the stage.

That can’t be allowed.

“HKS,” Mydei snarls, rolling to his feet.

Phainon is fast, but Mydei is faster, chasing him down the aisle. He leaps for Phainon, only for Phainon to jump not forward but to the side, landing on the back of a seated custodian’s chair. Nimbly, Phainon races along the backs of the seats, and Mydei, not to be undone, rushes after him.

“Coward!” Mydei shouts. “Pay the price that’s owed in blood!”

Violent strings, arpeggiated chords, blaring brass, the angry filigree of flutes and oboes. Music swirls in Mydei’s ears, drowning out his own furious cries as Phainon leaps into the aisle and sprints toward the stairs to the stage.

Mydei hurries after, leaping over the backs of seats. The custodians watch him, doing nothing to help him, and they should be helping him. Some primordial part of him knows they hear the music, too, but they are far too entertained by the show of Mydei chasing down Phainon.

Phainon gains the stairs, the stage. Mydei is right behind him, reaching, reaching—

Only for Phainon to whip around, zweihander drawn. His lips move, a threat dripping from them, the promise of violence between them, and Mydei throws one fist, two. Phainon deflects his punches with lightning-fast cuts of his sword, and they dance across the front of the stage. The music swells around them, the clanging of Phainon’s steel against Mydei’s own becoming the percussive rhythm of their song.

Wild, Mydei lashes out at Phainon, smacking aside his counterstrikes and ripostes, searching for the opening he needs to duck beneath Phainon’s guard, to rip out his throat like he should’ve done when they were on the floor in the aisle. Phainon has to die, has to pay, has to—

Phainon knocks aside one of Mydei’s punches, drops his shoulder, and barrels forward. They collide, and Mydei flies backwards, skidding across the stage, dazed. He can’t breathe, but he doesn’t need to breathe, he just needs Phainon to die.

Picking himself up off the ground, staggering to his feet, Mydei expects to find Phainon standing over him or at least nearby. Instead, Phainon stands in front of the lectern, a pen in his hand.

A book.

There’s a book on the lectern, and it’s open, and—and that matters. It terrifies him. Violins scream, clarinets shriek, the heavy beat of the drum compels Mydei to move. Phainon can’t be allowed to put that pen against that paper.

Mydei runs. He runs at Phainon, the music a furious symphony in his ears, in his head, and he’s crying but he doesn’t know why. He can’t lose this. He can’t lose what he has left, he can’t let Phainon—

put—

pen—

to—

paper—

Phainon writes.

And Mydei sees the fantasy for what it truly is.

“Thank you so much for coming,” the woman says, slipping her gloved fingers into Phainon’s.

Phainon lifts her hand and bends over it at the same time, pantomiming a kiss just above the back of it. He releases her as he straightens, finally and truly looking at her.

Worn, thin. Heavy lines around her face, hollow amber eyes. She wears a day dress of ivory linen and white lace, a pretty contrast to the fiery auburn of her hair. Not a beautiful woman but a handsome one worn down by grief and loss.

They’ve all been worn down by grief and loss.

She takes him up a flight of stairs and down long hallway, the gilt of it staggering. He can’t imagine her wealth. At the end of the hallway, a man stands like a sentinel before a half-open door, one sleeve pinned to his shoulder, his other hand holding a cane. When she and Phainon approach, he takes a step toward them, menacing, with fury in his eyes.

“I am not amenable to this,” he says.

“You are amenable to nothing,” she replies, lifting her chin. Despondent but not defeated. “We must at least try.”

He scoffs, pacing toward her where he stops, straight and stern, a military man wearing his faded colors. “We have tried. We have tried everything reasonable—”

She looks from him to Phainon and back again. “Eurypon,” she says, beseeching.

“—and now you bring one of them into our home.”

“Then perhaps it’s time to be unreasonable,” she says.

“This,” he hisses, “is an insult.”

She throws her hands into the air. “Then go! Do not stay. No one is forcing you to be here! With no recourse left to us, what should I choose? Should I condemn him to please you? I have nothing left!”

“You have me,” he says, his voice breaking.

Her expression is pitying, and Phainon, uncomfortable, hangs his head and tries to be as unobtrusive as possible.

Eurypon seethes. “I will not stand for this. I will have him thrown out of this house—my house, do you understand me, Gorgo?”

“You must do as you think right,” she says as he storms by her, deliberately walking his shoulder into Phainon’s as he passes. Eurypon’s sneer is familiar; Phainon has seen that expression so many times on so many faces. It shouldn’t have the power to hurt anymore, but it still does. “Forgive him. Please.”

No, he doesn’t think he will, but she needn’t know that.

“Through here,” she says, and she pushes open the door to the most remarkable atelier Phainon has ever seen, so different from his own working space in his cramped flat. The room, excepting the wall with the door, is circular, is massive, is entirely glassed in from floor to ceiling, like a greenhouse. And like a greenhouse, there are tables littered with pops of color, myriad canvases depicting impossible landscapes—some small enough to fit in his hand and others somewhat larger, though none overwhelmingly big. Those canvases, the ones that dwarf the tables, lean against cabinet drawers stained with pigment, against potted plants, against the windows themselves. A pungent, nutty scent pervades the space—linseed oil, as distinct as gunpowder.

At the far end of the atelier stands a framed canvas, and seated before it, a young man with red-gold hair pulled into a queue, his back to them. He wears only his shirt and vest, his jacket discarded over the back of a nearby chair, and he leans forward, as though studying the landscape intently. He doesn’t turn to acknowledge them. Only his shoulders move as he breathes.

Gorgo clasps her hands, and her expression is strained. “Mydei,” she says.

The man—Mydei—doesn’t react.
